title: Fast Versus Timely
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues leaders wrongly default to speed as an advantage when the real goal should be timeliness -- matching the pace of action to what a situation actually requires. Outside genuine emergencies, the author contends speed and timeliness are often inversely related, since a mediocre decision made in the right window can outperform a brilliant one made too early or too late. The piece emphasizes that good timing depends more on information quality than information quantity, and closes with the line that speed wins races while timing wins outcomes.
points: Outside genuine emergencies, speed and timeliness are often inversely related -- moving fast can actually make a leader less timely.
Decisions operate on a time-value curve: a mediocre decision made at the optimal moment can beat a brilliant one made too early or late.
Timeliness depends more on information quality than information quantity, so the best leaders focus on what's likely to change the conditions around a decision.
The closing framing: speed wins races, timing wins outcomes -- the best leaders move when it matters most, not simply first.
quotes: In emergencies, speed and timeliness are the same thing. In all other circumstances, speed without regard for what the situation requires is usually a mistake.
